strengths: Novel earphone-based hardware (NeuroBuds) enabling unobtrusive, long-term, cost-effective ExG monitoring—a practical breakthrough for data collection in the field
Substantial new dataset (DailySense) with 50 hours of free-living data and 20 hours spanning five human senses—first of its kind, larger than typical lab-based ExG benchmarks

Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 novel tasks and 4 public benchmarks with consistent improvements; thorough ablation studies and saliency analysis demonstrating task-relevant frequency band activation
Well-motivated problem formulation clearly identifying two real barriers in ExG research (lab-controlled data, task-specific designs) with concrete proposed solutions
Grounded physiological approach using 12 established frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma, EMG, EOG, ECG) rather than task-specific arbitrary filtering
Solid empirical results: 87.6% average F1 on DailySense; pre-training provides substantial 5.7% improvement on DailySense and consistent gains on all public benchmarks
Practical deployment feasibility demonstrated: 25ms inference latency and 3.6% memory usage on smartphone enables real-time on-device inference
Clear presentation with well-organized figures, comprehensive appendices, and detailed reproducibility information
weaknesses: Critical cross-subject generalization failure: 58.6% performance (vs. 87.6% within-session)—a 31% absolute drop that directly undermines claims of learning 'generalizable' and 'task-agnostic' representations; no investigation of causes or proposed solutions

Dataset scale insufficient for foundation model claims: 50 hours is modest compared to recent work (e.g., BrainWave uses clinical data at scale); only 22 subjects limits population diversity; Figure 6 shows classification saturates at ~30% of pre-training data, suggesting limited scaling potential

Limited core methodological novelty: fixed frequency band decomposition is standard signal processing; reconstruction-based pre-training is acknowledged as prior work; PiMT is primarily engineering contribution rather than algorithmic innovation

Critical design choices lack proper justification: (1) exactly 12 bands—no systematic ablation comparing other band counts; (2) frequency-first ordering claimed 'empirical' but no ablation provided; (3) loss weighting coefficients 'heuristically selected' rather than systematically tuned

Dataset unavailability undermines reproducibility: authors still 'working with legal team' to share DailySense; NeuroBuds hardware not readily available to other researchers; reproducibility statement insufficient without data/code access

Task-agnostic claim overstated: the 12 physiologically-motivated frequency bands are not task-agnostic; saliency analysis (Figure 4) shows different tasks heavily use different bands, making the approach implicitly task-specific in practice

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing comparisons with BrainWave (recent foundation model cited); no comparison with task-specific state-of-the-art for individual tasks; unclear if baselines use same backbone in 'without pre-training' experiments

Signal quality validation limited: relies entirely on downstream task performance rather than direct metrics (SNR, spectral analysis); no comparison with clinical-grade systems; electrode placement compromises some signals (partial vertical EOG)

Pre-training redundancy: six reconstruction tasks appear redundant; Table 4 ablations show modest impacts, especially for phase-based reconstructions; unclear if simpler approaches could be equally effective

Insufficient analysis of cross-subject generalization failure: no investigation of causes (subject demographics, physiological variability, device positioning); no proposed solutions or domain adaptation approaches despite being the paper's most critical limitation

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across DailySense (87.6% F1 with pre-training) and four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI Competition IV 2b)
Novel and practical hardware contribution: NeuroBuds enables unobtrusive free-living ExG collection (20g, $80 vs $10k-50k alternatives)
First dataset spanning five human senses with 50 hours free-living and 20 hours task-specific data, demonstrating superior transferability compared to larger controlled datasets (TUAR, TUSZ)

Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 downstream tasks, 4 public benchmarks, extensive ablations (tokenization, pre-training components, patch sizes), statistical significance testing, and saliency analysis
Well-motivated physiological approach: Fixed 12-band decomposition grounded in ExG knowledge enables adaptive task-relevant feature selection without explicit supervision
Practical system design considerations: On-device deployment analysis (25ms latency, 3.6% memory), frozen encoder evaluation, and cross-participant generalization testing
weaknesses: Critical cross-subject generalization failure: Performance drops 30% absolute (87.6% to 58.6%), fundamentally contradicting task-agnostic learning claims and limiting real-world deployment. Root causes not adequately analyzed or addressed
Dataset unavailability significantly hampers reproducibility and community impact; authors only 'working with legal team to determine possibility of sharing'

Limited technical novelty: PiMT is straightforward (fixed band decomposition + linear tokenization), Bidirectional-Mamba is existing architecture, reconstruction pre-training is standard—contribution is primarily engineering integration rather than methodological innovation

Limited demographic diversity and scale: Only 22 participants (ages 23-62, 16M/6F), 50 hours of pre-training data modest by foundation model standards, and pre-training data has some overlap with test participants

Hardware validation limited to 2 participants (~1 hour) with correlation of 0.71 against OpenBCI; formal comparison on larger cohort with clinical-grade equipment would strengthen signal quality claims

Misalignment between claims and results: Paper claims to enable 'task-agnostic ExG monitoring in the wild' but only demonstrates within-subject task-agnostic learning; cross-subject performance (58.6%) insufficient for practical deployment
Missing key comparisons with recent ExG foundation models (e.g., BrainWave mentioned but not compared); limited analysis of why task-agnostic tokenization does not improve cross-subject transfer

On-device deployment uses Transformer proxy instead of actual Mamba (unavailable on Android), so practical efficiency gains not demonstrated; gaze tracking accuracy (6.11°) not compared against traditional eye-tracking baselines

strengths: Novel hardware contribution (NeuroBuds): Compact, low-cost ($80) earphone-based ExG device enabling unobtrusive in-the-wild data collection, addressing a key bottleneck in ExG research
First multi-sense ExG benchmark (DailySense): 50 hours of free-living data + 20 hours of task-specific data spanning five human senses is a unique and valuable dataset resource

Well-motivated and physiologically grounded approach: The 12-band filter bank leverages established ExG physiology (EEG-delta, theta, etc.), with clear justification for multi-band decomposition to handle diverse task-specific frequency requirements

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Rigorous assessment on both DailySense and four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV 2b) with strong baselines and extensive ablations (pre-training components, tokenization methods, patch sizes, backbone architectures)

Consistent and significant empirical improvements: Average F1-score of 87.6% vs. 77.9% for Bidirectional-Mamba baseline with pre-training; improvements validated across diverse tasks with statistical significance testing

Interpretable learned representations: Saliency analysis (Figure 4) demonstrates that PiMT learns physiologically-relevant task-specific frequency patterns without explicit supervision, providing model transparency

Thorough reproducibility support: Detailed appendices covering hardware design, data collection protocols, implementation details, hyperparameter tuning, and hardware-software co-design considerations
Honest acknowledgment of limitations: Authors transparently discuss dataset scale, demographic diversity, cross-subject generalization challenges, and future research directions
weaknesses: Critical cross-subject generalization gap: Performance drops dramatically from 87.6% (within-subject) to 58.6% (cross-subject)—a 29% absolute drop—severely limiting real-world deployment potential for diverse users across different physiologies and sensor placements

Modest technical novelty: Core contributions are relatively incremental—fixed frequency band decomposition applies known physiology, Bidirectional-Mamba is existing architecture (Zhu et al., 2024), and reconstruction-based pre-training closely follows prior work (BIOT, BrainWave). Main value is systems integration rather than algorithmic innovation

Oversold 'task-agnostic' and 'foundation model' claims: The 12 fixed bands encode strong a priori physiological assumptions and are not learned/adapted; the approach is less task-specific than prior work but not truly agnostic. 50-hour pre-training dataset is far smaller than modern foundation models (billions of tokens)

Dataset not publicly available and has potential data leakage: DailySense remains unavailable ('working with legal team'); free-living and task-specific data come from same 22 participants, creating potential information leakage despite LOSO protocol (other subjects' data still informs task patterns)

Limited hardware validation: Signal quality validated against research-grade systems for only 2 participants (~1 hour); moderate correlation (0.71) with visible discrepancies in Figure 9; EMG and EOG modalities lack systematic validation against established benchmarks

On-device efficiency claims undermined: For smartphone deployment (Appendix N), Mamba replaced with Transformer due to lack of Android support; reported efficiency metrics use different architecture than main experiments, invalidating claims about on-device Mamba performance

Insufficient methodological justification: Token ordering chosen 'empirically' without ablation; λ weights for pre-training objectives selected heuristically rather than systematically; no justification for exactly 12 frequency bands despite diminishing returns curve suggesting saturation point unknown

Artificial task designs limit ecological validity: Taste/smell experiments involve controlled holding/sniffing for short durations rather than natural consumption; gaze evaluated against single eye tracker type; no evaluation on high-impact clinical applications (seizure detection, clinical sleep staging)
